Empirical Research Plan – “Colonial Rule and Long-Run Prosperity on Oceanic Islands”

=====================================================================

1. Identification Strategy
---------------------------
Strategy: Two–stage least‐squares instrumental-variables (IV) in a cross-section of 81 islands.

Rationale  
•  The key “treatments’’ (years under colonial rule, identity of coloniser, era of colonisation) are not randomly assigned.  
•  During 1500-1900 the feasibility of reaching an island was governed largely by prevailing winds. After ca. 1900 steamships broke the link between wind and economic activity, making wind conditions a plausibly exogenous historical shifter of colonial exposure that is no longer economically relevant today.  
•  Wind-based sailing difficulty therefore provides a powerful, plausibly exogenous instrument for colonial experience.  
•  DID/Event studies are infeasible (no long panel); an RDD would require a sharp policy cutoff that does not exist.

2. Treatment and Control
------------------------
Treatment variables (endogenous in second stage)

  T1. YearsUnderRule ≡ last_year_colony − first_year_colony  
  T2. Coloniser dummies: Britain, France, Spain/Portugal, Netherlands, United-States/Japan, Other (omitted = Britain).  
  T3. EarlyColonisation ≡ 1 if first settlement < 1700.  

Control group / counterfactual  
Because treatment is continuous, the counterfactual is islands that, conditional on controls, would have had shorter rule, later rule, or a different coloniser had the winds been less favourable.

Instrument(s)

  Z1. SailingSuitability ≡ mean (%) of months in which the great-circle bearing from Lisbon/Cádiz to island lay within ±20° of prevailing wind direction, weighted by wind speed, along the route up to 50°W.  
  Z2. LateralLongitudeError ≡ absolute longitudinal distance from Lisbon to first landfall along latitude of island (captures pre-chronometer navigation risk).  

Higher values of Z imply easier Age-of-Sail access → earlier contact and longer rule.

No timing dimension (cross-section), so no event date. No running variable (not RDD).

3. Key Identifying Assumptions
------------------------------
A1. Relevance: Wind-based instruments strongly predict colonial exposure.  
Plausibility: Historic navigation manuals and logbooks show that voyages clustered along prevailing easterlies/westerlies; discoveries match these corridors.

A2. Exclusion: Conditional on geographic controls (latitude, area, distance to continents, climate, hurricanes), Age-of-Sail wind patterns affect 2000 GDP or 2002 infant mortality only through colonial history.  
Plausibility: Steam eliminated sailing constraints ≈1900; wind at sea is unlikely to affect present-day production on tiny islands once we control for climate.

A3. Independence (as-good-as-random assignment): Wind patterns were fixed long before human settlement and are orthogonal to pre-contact island characteristics.  
Plausibility: Meteorological forces are exogenous to human and colonial decisions.

A4. Monotonicity: An island that becomes *easier* to reach because of better winds cannot end up with *less* colonial exposure (no defiers).  
Plausibility: Sailing technology constraints are one-sided.

A5. SUTVA: One island’s wind-driven colonial experience does not alter another island’s contemporary outcome except through standard general-equilibrium world-market channels (assumed negligible for small islands).

4. Main Threats and Mitigations
-------------------------------
Threat 1: Winds proxy for modern climatic zones (trade-wind tropics) that directly influence income via agriculture or disease.  
Mitigation: Add controls for mean temperature, precipitation, cyclone frequency, malaria ecology; run placebo on uncolonised islands (if any) to verify no direct wind-income link.

Threat 2: Measurement error in colonial dates (shipwreck settlements, informal rule) weakens first stage.  
Mitigation: Use multiple historical sources; instrument for *year of first permanent settlement* and *share of 1500-1900 years under rule*; cluster-robust standard errors.

Threat 3: Selective survival/sample—only islands that were eventually discovered enter the UN database.  
Mitigation: Show that wind instruments predict *year of discovery* in the universe of 160 candidate islands (including uninhabited rock outcrops) to demonstrate external validity; re-weight by inverse probability of inclusion.

5. R Code Outline
-----------------
```r
# 0. Packages -----------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast loading
library(fixest)       # IV regressions
library(sandwich)
library(lmtest)

# 1. Load data ----------------------------------------------------------
islands <- fread("islands_master.csv")   # 81×N dataset

# 2. Construct variables -----------------------------------------------
islands[, YearsUnderRule := last_year_colony - first_year_colony]

# Coloniser dummies
colonisers <- c("France","SpainPort","Netherlands","USJapan","Other")
for(c in colonisers){
  islands[, (paste0("col_",c)) := as.integer(coloniser==c)]
}

# Early colonisation
islands[, EarlyColonisation := as.integer(first_year_colony < 1700)]

# Instruments (already pre-computed or load)
wind <- fread("wind_sailing_suitability.csv")   # island_id, SailSuit, LonError
islands <- merge(islands, wind, by="island_id")

# Controls
controls <- c("log_area","abs_latitude","distance_continent",
              "mean_temp","mean_precip","cyclone_freq","log_population")

# 3. 2SLS main specification -------------------------------------------
fmla <- as.formula(paste(
  "log(GDP_pc_2000) ~ YearsUnderRule + col_France + col_SpainPort +",
  "col_Netherlands + col_USJapan + EarlyColonisation +",
  paste(controls, collapse=" + "),
  "| . | 0 | 0 | SailSuit + LonError"
))

iv_main <- feols(fmla, data=islands, vcov="HC1")
summary(iv_main, stage=1)  # shows first-stage F-stats

# 4. Robustness: add climate controls, use infant mortality -------------
fmla_imr <- update(fmla, log(GDP_pc_2000) ~ log(infant_mort_2002))
iv_imr <- feols(fmla_imr, data=islands, vcov="HC1")
summary(iv_imr, stage=1)

# 5. Over-identification Hansen test -----------------------------------
wald_iv(iv_main, param = ~ SailSuit + LonError, vcov = "HC1")
```

6. Expected Results
-------------------
Prior:

• Every additional 100 years of colonisation by *extractive Iberian* powers lowers 2000 GDP per capita by ≈15 % (≈0.15 log points) and raises infant mortality by ≈5 deaths/1,000.  
• British rule is neutral to mildly positive (≈ +0.05 log points).  
• Early (pre-1700) colonisation is associated with worse outcomes because of forced-labour and plantation systems.

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV Design)
-------------------------------------------------
C1: Instrument relevance – 1  
C2: Independence of instrument – 1  
C3: Exclusion restriction – 0 .5 (some concern about climate channels)  
C4: Monotonicity – 1  
C5: SUTVA/No interference – 1  

Total: 4.5 / 5

=====================================================================
This plan exploits plausibly exogenous wind-driven variation in colonial exposure to estimate the causal impact of colonisation length, timing, and identity on present-day prosperity.
